topic: The Curious Link: Elastic Collisions and the Digits of Pi
target_audience: High school students interested in physics and mathematics

outline.topic: The Curious Link: Elastic Collisions and the Digits of Pi
outline.target_audience: High school students interested in physics and mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisite: Elastic Collisions
sections.content: Define 1D elastic collisions. Explain conservation of momentum and kinetic energy. Introduce the scenario: a small block (mass m) hitting a large block (mass M) toward a wall.
sections.example: A toy car (m=1kg) hits a heavy crate (M=100kg) that is sliding toward a solid brick wall.

sections.title: The Collisional Setup
sections.content: Visualize the geometry. We track the number of collisions between two blocks (m and M) and a wall. As M becomes significantly larger than m, the number of collisions changes unexpectedly.
sections.example: Imagine a tiny hamster (m) bouncing between a giant sumo wrestler (M) and a wall. We count every 'thud' of the hamster.

sections.title: The Mathematical Mapping
sections.content: Introduce the mind-bending result: when M = 100^n * m, the total number of collisions is the first n+1 digits of Pi (π). Explain that the phase space of the system maps to the geometry of a circle.
sections.example: If the mass ratio is 1:100, there are exactly 31 collisions (3.1... the first digits of π).

sections.title: Visualizing the Unfolding
sections.content: Explain the trajectory in 2D space. The velocity of the blocks can be represented as a vector bouncing within a wedge. The angle of the wedge is defined by the mass ratio, effectively 'measuring' π.
sections.example: An animated 'bouncing light beam' inside a wedge where the beam hits the edges exactly π/θ times.

sections.title: Conclusion and Intuition
sections.content: Summarize how physical conservation laws act as a 'calculator' for transcendental numbers. Highlight that nature often hides mathematical constants in the most chaotic-looking mechanical systems.
sections.example: Summarizing the 'Sumo-Hamster' simulation: The heavier the wrestler, the more digits of π we reveal through the hamster's path.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Elastic Collisions
lecture_lines: Elastic collisions conserve momentum and kinetic energy.
A small block hits a large block.
The large block slides toward a wall.
These laws govern simple mechanical motion.
[Asset: ElasticCollisionDiagram]
animations: Show two blocks, small block (m) and large block (M), on a black background (#000000). Label them with text "m" and "M" in light cyan (#E0FFFF).
Animate the small block (m) moving toward the large block (M) to represent a collision. Add a visual flash effect at the point of impact.
Display the text "Conservation of Momentum: m*v1 + M*v2 = Constant" in white (#FFFFFF) above the blocks.
Display the text "Conservation of Energy: 0.5*m*v1^2 + 0.5*M*v2^2 = Constant" in white (#FFFFFF) below the conservation of momentum text.
Slow down the animation to highlight the exchange of kinetic energy and momentum between the blocks.

storyboard.title: The Collisional Setup
lecture_lines: We track collisions between two blocks and a wall.
Mass ratio changes the collision count.
The hamster hits the sumo wrestler.
animations: Create a scene with a wall on the left, a large block (M) in the middle, and a small block (m) between the wall and block M. Label them with "Wall", "M", and "m" in light yellow (#FFFFE0).
Animate block 'm' bouncing back and forth between the Wall and block M. Increment a collision counter text "Collisions: 0" in light green (#90EE90) on the screen.
Increase the size of block M to simulate a significantly larger mass. As M increases, show the small block 'm' bouncing significantly more frequently. Update the counter "Collisions: X" accordingly.

storyboard.title: The Mathematical Mapping
lecture_lines: Mass ratio 100^n gives n+1 digits of Pi.
System phase space maps to circular motion.
Collisions act as a digits calculator.
Pi emerges from simple physical rules.
[Asset: PiCollisionGraph]
animations: Display the equation "M = 100^n * m" on screen in bright blue (#00BFFF). Explain this is the mass ratio rule.
Display the number "31" in bold yellow (#FFD700) and link it to the first two digits of Pi (π) by showing "π ≈ 3.14159..." in white (#FFFFFF).
Visualize a circle on the screen with a line rotating inside it, showing how the phase space of the system maps to the circumference and geometry of a circle.

storyboard.title: Visualizing the Unfolding
lecture_lines: Represent velocities as vectors in 2D.
The wedge angle depends on mass ratio.
Light beams hit edges π/θ times.
The system measures Pi geometrically.
[Asset: WedgeAnimation]
animations: Draw two lines originating from a central point, forming a wedge with an angle θ determined by the mass ratio m/M. Use bright orange (#FFA500) for the lines.
Animate a small dot (the "light beam") bouncing between the two lines of the wedge. The path of the dot should leave a faint trail in light grey (#D3D3D3).
Show the count of bounces in the wedge alongside the value of π, demonstrating that the number of bounces relates to the ratio π/θ.
Slowly change the angle θ of the wedge to show how the trajectory and number of bounces change as the mass ratio shifts.
Highlight the final number of bounces and the corresponding digits of π with a glowing effect in bright magenta (#FF00FF).

storyboard.title: Conclusion and Intuition
lecture_lines: Nature hides constants in chaotic systems.
Conservation laws reveal deep mathematical truths.
Physics effectively calculates fundamental numbers.
animations: Display a summary text: "Conservation laws can calculate digits of π." in white (#FFFFFF).
Show the "Sumo-Hamster" simulation again, with a very large block M and a tiny block m, highlighting the massive number of bounces (representing many digits of π).
Conclude with the text "Mathematics hidden in chaos" fading in at the center of the screen in bold, light blue (#ADD8E6).
